extracted.intended_audience: mathematics education researchers, university mathematics instructors, and graduate students interested in undergraduate proof teaching/research
extracted.subtask_description: A scholarly review of research on proof and proving at the undergraduate level, summarizing conceptual frameworks, assessment models, teaching methods, and findings about student difficulties and expert practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: De Villiers' five functions of proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Proof as means of: (1) verification/conviction; (2) explanation; (3) systematization; (4) discovery; and (5) communication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these functions as different evaluative lenses: a proof may be strong for verification but weak explanatorily; consider which function is primary when judging pedagogical or disciplinary value (de Villiers, 1990).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hanna: proofs that only prove vs proofs that explain
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish between proofs that merely establish truth (only prove) and those that provide understanding (explain).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating proofs (especially pedagogically), value explanatory aspects — connections, motivations, and insight — not just formal correctness (Hanna, 1989/1990).

rubrics_metrics.name: Balacheff taxonomy of argument sophistication
rubrics_metrics.description: Four types of argumentative strategies representing increasing sophistication: (1) naïve empiricism (concluding from few confirming cases); (2) crucial experiment (examining a non-specific case to consider generalization); (3) generic example (proof rests on generalized class properties); (4) thought experiment (distance from specific actions to logical deduction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these categories to classify and assess students' argument types and their level of generalizable reasoning; they provide a progression target for development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alibert & Thomas: method of scientific debate (three steps)
rubrics_metrics.description: (1) Teacher initiates/organizes production of scientific statements (conjectures). (2) Students provide support/refutation by argument, proof, refutation, counterexample. (3) Statements confirmed by full demonstration become class-accepted theorems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a pedagogical rubric, evaluate classroom activities by whether they engage students in conjecture-generation, argumentation, and communal acceptance — not passive reading of textbook proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leron's structural (top-down modular) presentation of proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Arrange proofs in levels proceeding from top down; levels consist of short autonomous 'modules', each embodying a major idea of the proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess proof presentations for modular summaries and clear top-level ideas; note empirical tradeoffs — some students value summaries, others find module-jumping cognitively costly (Fuller et al., 2014).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to 'unpack' informal mathematical statements (Selden & Selden)
rubrics_metrics.description: Translate informally written mathematical statements into formal predicate-logic structure (e.g., converting 'For a < b, there is a c so that f(c)=y whenever f(a)<y< f(b)' into a quantified formula).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure students' unpacking accuracy as a predictor of their ability to construct and validate proofs; low unpacking success (e.g., 5–8.5% in studied samples) indicates serious barriers to proof construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Major sources of student difficulty in constructing proofs (Moore)
rubrics_metrics.description: Three primary difficulty sources: (a) concept understanding, (b) mathematical language and notation, (c) getting started on a proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these dimensions diagnostically when evaluating student work and designing instruction; interventions should target conceptual knowledge, facility with notation/language, and strategic entry into proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harel & Sowder's proof scheme categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Categories describing what individuals consider 'proof': (1) External conviction schemes — proof is what an authority/text says; (2) Empirical proof schemes — checking enough cases; (3) Analytical proof schemes — acceptable community proofs, including Transformational and Axiomatic schemes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify students' justificatory practices by these schemes to assess their epistemic stance toward proofs and their readiness for formal mathematical argumentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof validation ability as a distinct metric
rubrics_metrics.description: An individual's ability to determine the correctness of a proof (one's own or another's) — distinct from constructing or comprehending presented proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess validation separately (e.g., studies showed transition-to-proof students performed at chance on validation tasks); include tasks where students read and judge peer-generated arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof comprehension vs proof construction vs proof validation vs proof evaluation (Selden & Selden distinction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Different dimensions: comprehension (reading & learning from presented proofs), construction (creating novel proofs), validation (deciding correctness of proofs), and evaluation (grading/assessing proofs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When designing assessments or research, treat these as separate outcomes; a student may do well on one and poorly on others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mejía-Ramos et al. assessment model: state definitions in own words
rubrics_metrics.description: (1) State the definitions of terms used in the proof in their own words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Part of a multi-dimensional proof-comprehension assessment; tests whether students grasp term meanings contextually rather than merely reproducing formal definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mejía-Ramos et al. assessment model: identify trivial implications
rubrics_metrics.description: (2) Identify trivial implications of a given statement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assesses low-level logical understanding of immediate consequences inside the proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mejía-Ramos et al. assessment model: identify illustrative examples
rubrics_metrics.description: (3) Identify examples that illustrate a given term in the proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Checks ability to connect abstract terms to concrete instances used or suggested by the proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mejía-Ramos et al. assessment model: restate statements equivalently
rubrics_metrics.description: (4) Restate a given statement in a different, but equivalent, manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluates conceptual flexibility and recognition of equivalent formulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mejía-Ramos et al. assessment model: identify proof framework
rubrics_metrics.description: (5) Identify the type of proof framework (e.g., contradiction, contraposition).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tests recognition of high-level logical strategy used in the proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mejía-Ramos et al. assessment model: identify sentence purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: (6) Identify the purpose of a sentence within the proof framework.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assesses understanding of each line's role (assumption, lemma, instantiation, conclusion) in the overall argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mejía-Ramos et al. assessment model: make implicit warrants explicit
rubrics_metrics.description: (7) Make explicit an implicit warrant in the proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluates ability to spot and articulate unspoken logical links that justify inferential steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mejía-Ramos et al. assessment model: identify supporting data
rubrics_metrics.description: (8) Identify specific data supporting a given claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Checks ability to point to premises or examples that ground a particular inferential move.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mejía-Ramos et al. assessment model: identify dependent claims
rubrics_metrics.description: (9) Identify the specific claims that are supported by a given statement (e.g., which claims in the proof logically depend on a given line).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assesses understanding of logical dependency within the argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mejía-Ramos et al. assessment model: provide good proof summary
rubrics_metrics.description: (10) Provide a good summary of the proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tests ability to extract and communicate the core high-level idea(s) of the whole proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mejía-Ramos et al. assessment model: summarize sub-proof
rubrics_metrics.description: (11) Identify a good summary of a key sub-proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assesses ability to condense and explain important intermediate modules of the argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mejía-Ramos et al. assessment model: partition proof into modules
rubrics_metrics.description: (12) Partition the proof into modules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluates recognition of modular structure; links to structured/top-down presentations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mejía-Ramos et al. assessment model: identify module purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: (13) Identify the purpose of a module in the proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Checks whether students see why a module is included and what role it plays in the larger argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mejía-Ramos et al. assessment model: identify relations between modules
rubrics_metrics.description: (14) Identify the logical relation between modules of the proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assesses understanding of how sub-arguments combine (e.g., implication, case analysis, composition).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mejía-Ramos et al. assessment model: identify method of proof
rubrics_metrics.description: (15) Identify the method of proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tests recognition of techniques (e.g., proof by induction, extremal principle) and classification of the approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mejía-Ramos et al. assessment model: transfer method to another context
rubrics_metrics.description: (16) Transfer the method of proof to a different task.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assesses ability to generalize and apply the proof method beyond the original theorem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mejía-Ramos et al. assessment model: appreciate scope of method
rubrics_metrics.description: (17) Appreciate the scope of the method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluates meta-level understanding of when and where the method applies and its limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Semantic vs syntactic proof production (Weber & Alcock)
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinction between syntactic proof production (drawing inferences by manipulating symbolic formulae) and semantic proof production (using instantiations of mathematical concepts to guide formal inferences).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing students' proofs, note whether reasoning is driven by symbol manipulation or conceptual instantiation; many productive proofs involve a combination of both.

rubrics_metrics.name: Raman's notion of key ideas (public/private aspects of proof)
rubrics_metrics.description: Framework distinguishing public aspects of proof (what is presented) and private aspects (individual cognitive processes), linked by key idea(s) that make proofs meaningful to solvers and to readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate proofs (and teaching) by whether key ideas linking private reasoning to public presentation are highlighted and accessible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cognitive unity between conjecturing and proving
rubrics_metrics.description: The degree of continuity (cognitive unity) between processes of conjecturing and proving — whether the ideas used to conjecture reappear in the proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use cognitive-unity as a criterion for analyzing student work: high unity suggests integrated reasoning; low unity may indicate disconnection between exploration and formalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Toulmin scheme — limited suitability for proof construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Toulmin's argumentation concepts (claim, data, warrant, backing, modality, rebuttal) can analyze classroom argumentation and conjecturing but are less well-suited to formal proof construction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply Toulmin analysis for evaluating argumentative classroom discourse, conjectures, and pedagogical argumentation tasks rather than formal proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alcock: four modes of thinking of successful provers
rubrics_metrics.description: Successful provers use (1) instantiation (thinking about particular/generic objects), (2) structural thinking (using formal structure and deductions), (3) creative thinking (finding crux via examples/manipulations), and (4) critical thinking (checking correctness via counterexamples and implied properties).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess students' proofs and problem-solving by presence/absence of these modes; instruction can model and cultivate multiple modes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Features of good pedagogical proofs (Lai, Weber, Mejía-Ramos)
rubrics_metrics.description: Introductory and concluding sentences should be included; main ideas should be formatted/emphasized; extraneous or redundant information should be removed to avoid distraction or confusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When preparing proofs for teaching, explicitly include opening/closing statements, highlight key ideas, and pare unnecessary detail to aid student comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematicians' grading criteria for student proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Most important characteristics of a well-written proof: logical correctness, clarity, fluency, and demonstration of understanding; notation/layout/grammar often given less weight though noted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these dimensions to design rubrics and give feedback: correctness and evidence of understanding should dominate scoring; fluency issues can be addressed but may carry less scoring weight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inquiry-Based Learning (IBL) vs Inquiry-Oriented Instruction (IOI) pedagogical criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: IBL (social movement derived from Moore Method) emphasizes student-centered time for exploration and proving; IOI is rooted in mathematics-education theory, focusing on student thinking and designed activities to address difficulties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or choosing instruction, consider alignment with goals: IBL often focuses on developing proving skills and classroom social structures; IOI emphasizes theoretically grounded activities for concept development.

rubrics_metrics.name: DNR principles for teaching mathematical induction (Harel)
rubrics_metrics.description: DNR: Duality (distinguish ways of thinking vs ways of understanding), Necessity (students must see intellectual need), Repeated Reasoning (practice to interiorize ways of thinking).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use DNR as a teaching-design rubric for induction and similar topics: create intellectual need, distinguish conceptual from procedural understanding, and provide repeated reasoning practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structured proofs: tradeoffs for student readers
rubrics_metrics.description: Structured/top-down proofs provide summaries and modularization; empirical work shows some students value summaries whereas others complain they 'jump around' and require scanning to coordinate information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use structured proofs cautiously: include supports (e.g., pointers, maps) to help students coordinate modules; evaluate whether structuring aids or hinders comprehension for the target class.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of proofs that are often difficult for students
rubrics_metrics.description: Some proof techniques appear systematically harder for students (e.g., proof by contradiction, mathematical induction, recipe proofs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessments and instruction should give extra support and targeted tasks for these difficult proof types; consider conceptual and resource-activation explanations rather than only logical structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affect and nonemotional cognitive feelings in proving
rubrics_metrics.description: Nonemotional cognitive feelings (e.g., feelings of knowing, caution, familiarity, confusion, rightness of direction) and behavioural schemas (six-point sketch about availability, consciousness, action, chaining, dependence on conscious input, and acquisition through practice) influence proving.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider students' affective signals and behavioural schemas in assessment and instruction; feelings can guide productive action and need to be cultivated through practice and feedback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematicians' assessment of explanatory value and use of examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Expert judgments about how explanatory a proof is and how examples are used in proof-related activities influence what is valued in proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When designing rubrics or research tasks, include measures of explanatory value and the appropriateness/effectiveness of examples, as mathematicians differentiate along these axes.
